articles.title: Rohingya hope for justice as UN court prepares to rule on Myanmar genocide case
articles.excerpt: An activist who fled Myanmar’s 2017 military crackdown says a historic ruling must lead to real change for refugees
articles.fullText:
A Rohingya activist who fled Myanmar as a teenager hopes a landmark ruling by the United Nations’ highest court on Thursday will bring long-awaited recognition of her community’s suffering, she told Radio Free Asia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is set to rule Nov. 19 on whether Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention during a military crackdown against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017, which forced more than 730,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh.
Though she hopes for a favorable ruling, Lucky Karim, a Rohingya who escaped the violence at the age of 14 and is now a human rights activist, warned that justice will mean little without action to protect refugees and allow them to return home.
“For Rohingya to have a positive outcome, it will be a historic moment, a historic victory for us,” she told RFA, adding that such a ruling could also offer hope to other ethnic minority communities in Myanmar, where years of conflict and military repression have displaced millions of people.
Lucky Karim, in front row on the left, with classmates at a primary school in Hlaing Thi village, Maungdaw Township, Rakhine State.
(Lucky Karim) Originally from Hlaing Thi village in Rakhine State’s Maungdaw township, Karim spent six years in a refugee camp in Bangladesh. In 2022, she founded Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, an organization advocating for the rights and education of Rohingya women.
Her hopes reflect the significance of a case that has taken seven years to reach a judgment and could establish Myanmar’s legal responsibility for one of the worst episodes of mass displacement in recent decades.
What happened to the Rohingya?
The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority from Myanmar’s western Rakhine State who have faced decades of discrimination, restrictions on movement and denial of citizenship in the Buddhist-majority country.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it described as clearance operations after Rohingya militants attacked security posts. Soldiers were accused of killing civilians, raping women and burning entire villages, driving hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.
A United Nations fact-finding mission later concluded that there were reasonable grounds to infer genocidal intent behind the military campaign and called for senior military officials to be investigated and prosecuted.
Myanmar has rejected accusations of genocide, maintaining that its operations were legitimate responses to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, a Rohingya insurgent group.
The Gambia, a small West African nation, brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the backing of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
It accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention, an international treaty adopted after World War II that obliges countries to prevent and punish genocide.
A view of the Great Hall of Justice, the courtroom of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, June 18, 2026. (Nicolas Economou/Reuters)
(Reuters) The ICJ ordered Myanmar in January 2020 to take measures to prevent genocidal acts against the Rohingya and preserve evidence.
Myanmar’s government filed objections to the case in January 2021, just days before the country’s military took control of the country in a coup.
The court rejected the objections in 2022, and held hearings on the allegations in January this year.
During those hearings, The Gambia argued that the pattern of killings, sexual violence and destruction demonstrated an intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group. Myanmar’s military government disputed that interpretation, arguing that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold required to establish genocide.
What could the ruling change?
Thursday’s judgment will determine whether Myanmar bears responsibility under international law for violations of the Genocide Convention.
Unlike the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals, the ICJ settles disputes between countries. Its ruling cannot directly send military commanders to prison or compel the immediate return of refugees.
But a finding against Myanmar would carry legal and diplomatic weight and could require the country to take further measures to address violations and provide reparations.
For Karim, the distinction between a legal victory and improvements in refugees’ lives is crucial.
“The judgment from the International Court of Justice does not immediately change the ground reality. It doesn’t immediately repatriate refugees from refugee camps to Burma either,” she said, using Myanmar’s former name.
The challenges facing the Rohingya have only deepened since the 2017 crackdown.
After the 2021 coup, the country was plunged into a wider civil war. Renewed fighting in Rakhine State between the military and the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has exposed Rohingya civilians to further violence and displacement.
The United Nations said in May that approximately 150,000 Rohingya had arrived in Bangladesh since early 2024, adding to the pressure on already overcrowded refugee settlements.
Around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees were living in Bangladesh, according to the UN’s May estimate, most of them in and around Cox’s Bazar, home to one of the world’s largest refugee settlements.
Their return to Myanmar remains fraught with uncertainty, with concerns over safety, citizenship rights and protection from persecution still unresolved.
Lucky Karim is seen in front of the house where he lived in refugee camp number 8 in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, in March 2019.
(Lucky Karim) “Until it is safe for everyone, it’s not safe for any one of us in Burma,” Karim said.
She urged governments and international organizations to ensure that any judgment leads to concrete measures to protect refugees and create conditions for their safe, voluntary and dignified return.
The ICJ’s judgments are legally binding, although the court has no independent enforcement force. If a country fails to comply, the other party may seek action through the UN Security Council.
Karim said achieving lasting change would require sustained international commitment and the implementation of the court’s ruling, rather than simply recognizing the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.
“So the judgment should not be a piece of paper,” she said. “It shouldn’t be another genocide declaration.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit puts nuclear arms control, North Korea in focus
articles.excerpt: Analysts see little prospect of a nuclear deal, while Pyongyang hopes its allies will press its case with the US.
articles.fullText:
When U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit , a concrete agreement on nuclear arms control would be an unlikely result, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
The meeting comes as Washington seeks to bring Beijing into nuclear discussions with Moscow, while China maintains that its smaller arsenal makes participation in such negotiations unreasonable. North Korea, meanwhile, is closely monitoring the meeting for any implications it might have for its own nuclear weapons program.
Though a deal is not likely, the summit could open channels for further consultations on nuclear risks, Cheng Xiaonong, a U.S.-based Chinese scholar, told RFA Mandarin.
“My understanding is that Trump is essentially trying to use Putin to teach Xi Jinping a lesson,” he said. “Of course, Putin will want to negotiate something in return.”
U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping stands beside, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026.
(Iori Sagisawa/Reuters) Trump is scheduled to meet Xi bilaterally before joining Putin for trilateral talks. Discussions are expected to include nuclear disarmament or the wars in Ukraine and Iran, although China has not released a detailed agenda.
North Korea, which maintains close ties with both Beijing and Moscow, has not publicly commented on the summit, but analysts say Pyongyang may hope its allies will use the meeting to advance its longstanding demands for recognition as a nuclear-armed state and relief from international sanctions.
Competing nuclear interests
The United States and Russia have decades of experience negotiating nuclear arms control agreements, but China has resisted joining similar negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal remains substantially smaller.
Cheng said that China’s continued nuclear expansion and reliance on strategic deterrence would make a trilateral agreement difficult.
He said Washington would seek a commitment from Xi to restrain China’s nuclear arsenal, while Beijing and Moscow would pursue their own objectives in negotiations with Trump.
“All three have their own calculations, and they can’t work together,” Cheng said. “Under those circumstances, a joint statement would be meaningless.”
Spectators wave Chinese flags as military vehicles carrying DF-41 nuclear ballistic missiles roll during a parade to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the founding of Communist China in Beijing, Oct. 1, 2019.
(Mark Schiefelbein/AP) Xi will likely use the summit to demonstrate China’s status as a major power and strengthen his domestic political authority, Song Guocheng, a Taiwanese international relations scholar, told RFA Mandarin.
He also considered a concrete nuclear arms control agreement unlikely but said the leaders could still make progress on reducing nuclear risks.
The leaders “could establish what we call a nuclear weapons communication mechanism, with emergency procedures or arrangements between them,” Song said. “That could at least help prevent nuclear miscalculations.”
China’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that the leaders would exchange views on maintaining world peace and promoting strategic stability among major powers.
Beijing has previously said requiring China to participate in trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage would be neither reasonable nor realistic.
North Korea seeks recognition, fears concessions
For North Korea, analysts say the summit could provide an opportunity to seek diplomatic support for its nuclear ambitions, although Pyongyang is not participating in the talks.
North Korea likely hopes that China and Russia will convey Pyongyang’s demands to Trump, Kim Tae-woo, a former president of the Seoul-based Korea Institute for National Unification, told RFA Korean.
“North Korea essentially has two demands and expectations when it comes to nuclear weapons,” Kim said. “The first is recognition of its status as a nuclear-armed state. The second is that any nuclear talks with the United States must be conducted as arms reduction negotiations between nuclear powers on an equal footing.”
Analysts said an explicit endorsement of North Korea’s nuclear status was unlikely, but the absence of calls for denuclearization could still be welcomed by Pyongyang.
This image distributed by the North Korean government on March 24, 2022, and not independently verifiable shows leader Kim Jong Un walking away from what state media reports as a "new type" of intercontinental ballistic missile.
(KCNA via Reuters) “North Korea will hope that there are no statements about stability on the Korean Peninsula or North Korea’s denuclearization,” Shin Beom-chul, South Korea’s former vice minister of national defense, told RFA Korean. “They will be satisfied as long as denuclearization is not discussed.”
North Korea may also hope Beijing and Moscow will press Washington to ease sanctions, analysts said.
In December 2017, the U.N. Security Council – which includes Russia and China – adopted Resolution 2397, which imposed tighter restrictions on North Korea’s petroleum supplies, exports and overseas workers.
The summit could present risks for Pyongyang if China or Russia uses their relationships with North Korea as leverage.
Recent high-level diplomatic exchanges between North Korea and its neighbors might be showing Pyongyang’s concerns about being sidelined, Ko Young-hwan, a former president of South Korea’s National Institute for Unification Education, told RFA Korean.
“The war in Ukraine won’t go on forever,” Ko said. “North Korea is probably worried that China and Russia might do something with the United States behind its back.”
South Korea’s presidential office has said Seoul’s position and interests must be fully reflected in discussions among the three powers.
Prospects for further talks
Beyond nuclear arms control, analysts differ on whether the summit could lead to a more permanent diplomatic framework among Washington, Beijing and Moscow.
A scholar of U.S.-China relations identified only as Mr. Xing told RFA Mandarin that the meeting could signal the emergence of a “new Yalta system,” referring to the 1945 conference at which Allied leaders discussed the postwar international order.
Members of the "Art Lift" collective carry the artwork showing U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping next to the 'Big Three' monument with the leaders at the 1945 Yalta conference - Joseph Stalin, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill, in Livadia park in Yalta, Crimea, Nov. 16, 2026.
(Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters) Xing predicted the summit would remain largely symbolic, with China unlikely to support a formal consultation mechanism.
The U.S.-based Arms Control Association said ahead of the meeting that a single summit was unlikely to produce a major breakthrough, but the leaders could instruct negotiating teams to begin sustained discussions on nuclear arms limits and risk reduction.
The Kremlin said the parties were discussing a possible joint communiqué. If they cannot agree on a text, the three leaders will issue separate assessments of the talks.
Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Smiles and hugs ahead of Trump, Xi and Putin’s highly anticipated meeting
articles.excerpt: Shenzhen – China’s tech capital – rolls out the red carpet for the 33rd APEC summit.
articles.fullText:
SHENZHEN, China – U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the bottom of the stairs of Air Force One upon landing in China on Wednesday for this week’s APEC summit.
Both leaders embraced on the red carpet at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport as a crowd of women waved American flags and chanted “warm welcome” in Mandarin. Trump had just flown in from Manila where he had attended the ASEAN summit. The scene echoed Trump’s welcome at Joint Base Andrews at the start of Xi’s state visit to the United States in September.
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes U.S. President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China Nov. 18, 2026.
(Carlos Barria/Reuters) Shenzhen is hosting leaders from 21 Asia-Pacific economies during the two-day summit, but the scheduled meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday is the highly anticipated event.
The planned talks – to be held at Shenzhen’s lakeside Kylin Villa – echo the February 1945 summit of Britain’s Winston Churchill, the Soviet Union’s Joseph Stalin and U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in Yalta, months before the end of World War II.
“He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters about the meeting last week.
Trump later arrived at the venue of the APEC dinner, pausing to enjoy a rendition of “America the Beautiful” by a Chinese string and woodwind ensemble before being greeted by Xi and Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan.
Servers prepare for a welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026.
(Maxim Shemetov/AFP) As leaders gathered for the APEC family photo ahead of the dinner, a smiling Putin walked up to Trump and extended his hand as Xi looked on.
At the dinner, Xi took the stage and offered a toast to the “shared prosperity” of the Asia-Pacific region.
Shenzhen sparkles
As host city to the 33rd meeting of APEC economic leaders, China’s tech capital was on full display Wednesday. Promotional signage adorned the airport, many buildings and roadways. Flags decorated the trees and lampposts, giving the entire city a festive atmosphere.
A woman walks past a decorative sign for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 16, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) The streets were pristine, with everything meticulously organized, as if the city was eager to showcase its rapid development.
At the same time, police were stationed throughout the city to control traffic and ensure security. A heavy police presence was also evident around the International Media Center, where journalists from across the globe had gathered.
To enter the center, journalists passed through security checkpoints and were subject to rigorous screening; their photographs automatically appeared on a screen as they underwent baggage inspections and body searches, reflecting a strict emphasis on security protocols.
Security agents guard the hotel where U.S. President Donald Trump will stay during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov 18, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) Amid these measures, numerous volunteers were stationed on the shuttle buses connecting hotels to the media center, as well as inside the hotels and the media center itself, to assist journalists and other attendees.
The two-day summit ends Thursday, after which Trump is scheduled to immediately return to the U.S.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Xi hails Shenzhen's openness "DNA" at welcome banquet
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday hosted a banquet in Shenzhen to welcome guests attending the…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday hosted a banquet in Shenzhen to welcome guests attending the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders' Meeting.

"I wish to extend, on behalf of the Chinese government and the Chinese people, our warmest welcome to all distinguished guests," Xi said in his toast.

Openness is deeply rooted in Shenzhen's DNA and innovation drives the city's vitality, while cooperation is where its strength comes from, Xi said, adding that the success of Shenzhen is also a microcosm of China's reform and opening up, as well as an example of fruitful cooperation across the Asia-Pacific.

Noting that openness, innovation and cooperation have been the distinctive features of Apec since its establishment, Xi said Apec has grasped the pulse of the times and guided the process of regional economic integration, making the Asia-Pacific the most dynamic region and a vital growth engine of the world economy.

"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss steps to expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields," Xi said.

Before the banquet, Xi and Peng posed for group photos with leaders and representatives from Apec economies and their spouses.

After the banquet, they joined the guests to watch an artistic performance. (Xinhua)

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
articles.excerpt: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs…
articles.fullText:
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .

You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

articles.title: "A Symphony of Lights" goes out on a high
articles.excerpt: The long-running multimedia spectacle that lights up Victoria Harbour every night has drawn to a close, after its last performance…
articles.fullText:
The long-running multimedia spectacle that lights up Victoria Harbour every night has drawn to a close, after its last performance on Wednesday.

Scores of locals and tourists lined the promenade in Tsim Sha Tsui to catch the finale of "A Symphony of Lights" at 8pm, with some arriving an hour early to secure a good vantage position.

Light installations at more than 40 buildings along both sides of Victoria Harbour, including Central Plaza, the Convention and Exhibition Centre, as well as One and Two ifc, lit up the skies in the 10-minute show.

Fireworks were also launched from several high-rise buildings.

Among those who turned up was a SAR resident who brought his foreign friends to watch the show.

"The light show is quite nice; this is spectacular," he said. "But we are quite sad this is the last day."

Another tourist who visited Hong Kong for the first time said she was lucky to catch the show at the last opportunity.

Tourism minister Rosanna Law said the added pyrotechnic elements gave the show a perfect ending.

"In 2005, 'A Symphony of Lights' was recognised by the Guinness World Records as the world's largest permanent light and sound show, and it was among the world's first large-scale light shows performed nightly - showcasing the magnificent night view of Victoria Harbour to countless residents and visitors over the years," she said.

Law spoke at the launch ceremony of Hong Kong WinterFest 2026, which runs through Christmas and the New Year.

As part of the seven-week festival, light shows would be projected onto iconic building facades in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui between 7pm and 11pm every night.

Edited by Raymond Yeung

articles.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.

How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?

—Amit Katwala

Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.

Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power .

—Casey Crownhart

MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid .

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple
The agency’s classified communications network has gone down. ( CNN )
+ An update disrupted Apple Music, App Store, and AppleCare. ( AP )
+ The issues join a recent flood of outages at critical services. ( CNBC )
+ Marco Rubio says they’re unrelated and not hostile acts. ( Guardian )
+ But AI is accelerating the discovery of vulnerabilities. ( Vox )
+ And making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Measles is officially endemic again in the US
Scientists blame persistent gaps in vaccination coverage. ( Guardian )
+ This year’s outbreak is the deadliest since 1991. ( Nature )
+ Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status. ( DW )
+ Other infections could be next. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 Only nine countries have backed COP31’s AI climate pledge
The voluntary pledge doesn’t include binding targets. ( Reuters $)
+ Plans for carbon removal tech have divided COP31. ( New Scientist $)
+ For all its flaws, the annual climate meeting still matters. ( Axios )
+ What to know about this year’s talks. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Nvidia has delivered blowout results and rejected Huang’s return
Revenue more than doubled amid booming AI chip sales. ( Axios )
+ Nvidia has stopped shipments of H200 chips to China. ( Gizmodo )
+ China has threatened countermeasures over new chip curbs . ( Reuters $)

5 More than a third of Gen-Z relies on AI for friendship
Those who do have higher odds of loneliness. ( Wired $)

6 Ukraine says Starshield speed limits remain in occupied territory
Zelenskyy said the restrictions hamper air defences. ( CNBC )

7 San Diego has dumped Flock cameras and smart streetlights
It’s shutting down more than 500 surveillance cameras. ( Ars Technica )
+ What Flock’s defenders are missing. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Waymo has pulled its driverless taxis from US freeways
The move comes after California banned freeway trips. ( NBC News )

9 Lakes are becoming strangely synchronized
Scientists warn this could lead to ecological collapses. ( 404 Media )

10 “Human” has won the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year
The dictionary says the word has gained importance in the AI age. ( BBC )

Quote of the day

“ It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

—Donald Trump shrugs off a week of outages that grounded flights, locked customers out of their banks, and knocked out an NSA network, NPR reports .

One more thing

SARAH ROGERS/MIT TECHNOLOGY REVIEW | GETTY IMAGES

What’s next for IVF

IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that. 

Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease.

The technologies could make IVF more effective and accessible. But they’re also raising difficult ethical questions about how far reproductive medicine should go.

Here’s what’s next for IVF .

—Jessica Hamzelou

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ One man’s mom has made him a magnificent Monty Python and the Holy Grail quilt .
+ An origamist has folded an astonishing mechanical typewriter from a single sheet of paper.
+ The Techno-Optimism Archive is a fascinating history of hype surrounding new technologies.
+ This richly illustrated travelogue traces the curious journey of citrus from the Himalayan foothills to the heart of Sicily.

articles.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
articles.excerpt: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working…
articles.fullText:
In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

OSMO AI

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication. 

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies .

For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

articles.title: Local stocks close lower
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong's stock market ended lower on Wednesday, with the benchmark Hang Seng Index down 0.91 percent to close at…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong's stock market ended lower on Wednesday, with the benchmark Hang Seng Index down 0.91 percent to close at 23,294 points.

The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index dropped 0.86 percent, and the Hang Seng Tech Index slid 0.58 percent.

On the mainland, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index finished up 0.09 percent while the Shenzhen Component Index closed 0.2 percent higher.

In Japan, Tokyo stocks ended mixed, as stronger-than-expected earnings from US chipmaker Nvidia lifted investor sentiment, while lingering uncertainty over the artificial intelligence sector kept risk appetite in check.

The Nikkei ended up 163 points, or 0.28 percent, at 59,024.

The broader Topix index, meanwhile, fell 16 points, or 0.42 percent, to close at 3,824.

Japanese stocks fluctuated throughout the day as investors weighed optimism over Nvidia's latest earnings against persistent concerns about the outlook for AI-related stocks.

Nvidia reported record quarterly net profit and revenue, easing concerns over the profitability and sustainability of massive investments in AI infrastructure.

However, uncertainty surrounding the company's leadership transition following Jensen Huang's departure, along with concerns over potential AI regulations in the United States, continued to weigh on investor sentiment. (Xinhua)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Xi welcomes Trump in Shenzhen
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump was welcomed with a hug by President Xi Jinping as he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump was welcomed with a hug by President Xi Jinping as he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday afternoon to attend this year's Apec summit.

Xi greeted Trump upon his arrival at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport.

The president told the US leader that he wanted a "constructive, strategically stable relationship" between China and the United States.

"I look forward to an in-depth exchange of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape, with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations – one built upon the foundations of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity," Xi said.

On Thursday, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will hold a landmark summit on the Apec sidelines to discuss safeguarding world peace.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine as well as nuclear disarmament are expected to be on the agenda. (Agencies)

articles.title: CE holds bilateral talks at Apec summit
articles.excerpt: Chief Executive John Lee on Wednesday held a series of meetings on the sidelines of the Apec summit, promoting Hong…
articles.fullText:
Chief Executive John Lee on Wednesday held a series of meetings on the sidelines of the Apec summit, promoting Hong Kong's role as a gateway to Greater Bay Area and the mainland to regional leaders.

During his meeting with Vietnam's President To Lam, Lee said bilateral trade between Hong Kong and Vietnam grew by 75 percent last year.

"I'm glad that since we last met two years ago, trade and people-to-people ties have been growing strongly," Lee told the Vietnamese leader.

"Thanks to your excellent support... I think we have established a very strong foundation for greater growth between our two places."

Lee said he briefed the Vietnamese leader on the latest developments in Hong Kong, including the city's strengths as an international innovation and technology centre as well as development opportunities in the Greater Bay Area.

The Vietnamese president commended Hong Kong's socio-economic development and said the city was an important leading economic, financial and trade hub of the world.

In a Facebook post, Lee said he also met with Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah of Brunei.

He said Hong Kong and Brunei enjoy close commercial and people-to-people ties, and that bilateral trade in goods rose 40 percent last year.

Lee said Hong Kong's first five-year plan and the Northern Metropolis are injecting strong growth impetus into the city, and he welcomed Bruneian enterprises to seize the opportunities.

"I hope that Hong Kong can actively play the roles of a 'super connector' and 'super value-adder' to help Bruneian businesses explore business opportunities while connecting mainland enterprises with partners in Brunei, achieving mutually beneficial outcomes," he wrote.

"In addition, I encourage more friends from Brunei to visit Hong Kong to experience our comprehensive Muslim-friendly tourism facilities as well as the unique charm of East-meets-West culture in Hong Kong."

During his meeting with Thailand's Prime Minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, Lee encouraged Thai enterprises to set up operations in Hong Kong.

He thanked Thailand for its continued support of Hong Kong's early accession to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).

Lee said Hong Kong would continue to dedicate efforts to deepening bilateral cooperation in areas including trade, finance, and culture to jointly seize new opportunities in regional development.

Later on Wednesday, Lee met Chilean President José Antonio Kast, with the two leaders witnessing the signing of an agreement to establish a bilateral working holiday scheme.

The SAR leader said the arrangement would enable young people from both sides to broaden their horizons and deepen mutual understanding.

articles.title: Doctor 'zoned out' in wrong ovary removal: CUHKMC
articles.excerpt: CUHK Medical Centre on Wednesday said a doctor who had mistakenly removed a patient’s ovaries “zoned out” during the operation…
articles.fullText:
CUHK Medical Centre on Wednesday said a doctor who had mistakenly removed a patient’s ovaries “zoned out” during the operation in September.

The private hospital’s chief executive officer, Chung Kin-lai, apologised at a press conference, which was held a day after the hospital said in a statement that the doctor was highly focused on executing clinical steps and had "a temporary collapse of his situational awareness".

Chung said the patient’s operation – laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy – had two surgical options, either preserving or removing the ovaries, and the patient had chosen to keep her ovaries.

"The doctor, for a brief moment, failed to realise the step that should have been taken and was essentially acting on instinct," he said.

"In plain language that the general public can understand, you could basically say the doctor was absent-minded or zoned out, and carried out another option rather than the one chosen by the patient."

Chung added the doctor had immediately apologised to the patient, who was shocked and disappointed.

But the patient still chose to trust the doctor and was still attending consultations, he said.

Chung also said the doctor involved in the incident was a contract obstetrician-gynecologist who was experienced, well-respected in the sector and had a good reputation among patients.

He added the doctor had admitted the mistake, and the hospital would impose disciplinary actions according to its human resource policies.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Operator to pay HK$1.3m over parking meter failure
articles.excerpt: The operator of the on-street metered parking system has committed an indemnity of about HK$1.3 million to the government over…
articles.fullText:
The operator of the on-street metered parking system has committed an indemnity of about HK$1.3 million to the government over a territory-wide malfunction earlier this month.

In an oral reply to a Legco question, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the operator had also arranged to refund parking meter fees paid by users during the incident.

About 11,000 parking meters across the city failed to work properly for nearly four hours on November 3 due to a defective software update.

"Taking into account of the incident duration, the operator has committed an indemnity of about HK$1.3 million to the government," Chan said.

She said the operator had since strengthened real-time monitoring and introduced daily system health checks, and had committed to conducting high-intensity load tests in a staging environment simulating actual operating conditions before rolling out future updates, and to exploring phased implementation starting with small-scale trials.

To prevent a recurrence, Chan said the Transport Department has worked with the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department to review the system's engineering design and modify management procedures.

She said the Transport Department would carry out its next round of comprehensive security risk assessment and audit in December.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Xi, Putin meet ahead of historic summit with Trump
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday that relations between Beijing and Moscow have brought greater stability and certainty to a…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday that relations between Beijing and Moscow have brought greater stability and certainty to a world of turbulence and transformation in a meeting with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders gathering.

The meeting comes a day ahead of an historic three-way summit with US leader Donald Trump.

Xi told Putin that China-Russia relations have maintained a long-term perspective, providing greater stability and certainty to a rapidly changing world.

"Under the firm guidance of Mr. President and myself, China-Russia relations have remained as solid as a mountain, undaunted by wind and rain, while maintaining a long-term perspective and providing greater stability and certainty to an increasingly complex and rapidly changing world," he said.

Putin, for his part, said bilateral relations are firmly on track.

“Mutual trade between our countries has surpassed US$200 billion. This is the goal we set for ourselves. And it looks like this year it won’t only be reached once again but will also show a good dynamic. In a complex geopolitical situation we are keeping constructive approaches in forming more just and multipolar world order."

Wednesday's meeting is the fifth time the two leaders have met this year, including once by video link.

Addressing the Apec CEO Summit earlier in the day, the Russian president said he expected the trilateral summit with Xi and Trump to be "highly useful".

"At a time when military-political risks are on the rise, what is desperately needed is unity rather than division... and dialogue rather than ultimatums," Putin said.

He said Western sanctions imposed on Russia since the beginning of the conflict with Ukraine had failed, arguing that they were "not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying the economies of the competition".

China has said that the three leaders on Thursday would hold "in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations".

Washington had signalled that Ukraine was not expected to be addressed, before Trump said that it would.

Also up for discussion are the Iran war and nuclear disarmament, according to US officials, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February. (Agencies)

Chief Executive John Lee said he had been inspired and encouraged by President Xi Jinping's speech at the Apec CEO summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday, adding the address had charted a course for the Asia-Pacific community and provided China's response to the challenges of the new era.

In a Facebook post, Lee cited Xi as saying that the Greater Bay Area economy is marked by distinctive openness and synergy.

He said Hong Kong can serve as a springboard for global businesses entering the Greater Bay Area and the mainland.

The government would also continue to use an established task force to help mainland enterprises expand in international markets and better seize bay area opportunities.

"With the strong backing of the country, let us continue to leverage the strengths of Hong Kong and the bay area, persist in deep integration and common development with all parties through openness, and help the country become a core force leading Asia-Pacific cooperation," he wrote.

articles.title: 'HK has key role in keeping global shipping stable'
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong will play an important part in keeping world shipping stable and fast-tracking the sector's green transition, said John…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong will play an important part in keeping world shipping stable and fast-tracking the sector's green transition, said John Denholm, chairman of the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), in a recent interview with Xinhua.

"The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area is a fantastic economic engine. I'm sure that Hong Kong, as a main port in the Greater Bay Area, will grow from strength to strength," Denholm told Xinhua on the sidelines of the World Maritime Merchants Forum 2026.

Hong Kong's commitment to free trade made it a popular place to do business, Denholm said.

It is also a staunch supporter of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea as well as the International Maritime Organisation's regulatory framework, which are essential to making world trade flourish, especially when heightened geopolitical tensions jeopardise freedom of navigation, said Denholm.

Denholm also applauded Hong Kong's pledge to advance the green transition of shipping.

The city aims to see the proportion of its registered vessels using green maritime fuels reach seven percent by 2030.

Denholm expects the use of green fuels to grow fast as the shipping industry is committed to achieving net-zero emissions by around 2050.

Hong Kong is poised to make green maritime fuel more available to the industry with the support of the world-leading shipbuilding capacity and green technologies of the Chinese mainland, according to Denholm.

In the first three quarters of this year, Chinese shipyards secured 81.8 percent of the world's new shipbuilding orders.

China also has the potential to become a major supplier of green fuel, said Denholm.

At the opening ceremony of the World Maritime Merchants Forum 2026 on Monday, Hong Kong inked an agreement with the Port of Piraeus in Greece to jointly establish a Green Shipping Corridor.

Denholm called Hong Kong's partnership with other ports to provide clean fuel a "fantastic start" to promote the green revolution. (Xinhua)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Alaska Democrat flips US Senate seat in tight race
articles.excerpt: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit…
articles.fullText:
Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state US President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.

The Alaska race is the last US Senate contest to be resolved in this year's midterm elections, and Peltola’s victory expands the Democrats’ majority after they retook control of the chamber.

The party already won campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and, most recently, Mississippi.

With Peltola’s victory, Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most since 1958.

Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, while Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin.

Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, after former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by Trump.

The Associated Press has not yet called the US House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Representative Nick Begich.

Flipping Alaska's seat was pivotal to Democrats' plans to retake the Senate.

Peltola previously held the state's lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress.

She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.

In the campaign’s final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent.

Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the November 3 election.

Peltola denied any involvement.

“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election.

Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats' behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since The Times’ article was published.

The candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan roiled the race.

The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year’s open primary and later sought to recant her statements.

But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump’s mind.

He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October.

Later, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered.

It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit “flagrant corruption.”

The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed.

Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election “without unwarranted interference by the United States.”

They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska’s ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them.

During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs.

Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are often only accessible by air or water.

Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of “Alaska first.”

“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said.

“I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”

Peltola will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate.

The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014. (AP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: South China Sea code of conduct could depend on landlocked Laos: analysts
articles.excerpt: ASEAN meetings again ended without a code of conduct, and Vientiane might have influence in future negotiations.
articles.fullText:
Landlocked Laos could play a huge role in future negotiations between ASEAN and China on a South China Sea code of conduct, potentially tipping the scales for Beijing, but close ties with its northern neighbor do not mean that Vientiane is acting as a proxy to block negotiations, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
As the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, concluded their summit in Manila this week, the bloc again failed to finalize the code of conduct, or COC – an agreement that would seek to prevent confrontations in the sea which is claimed in its entirety by China and in part by Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei and Malaysia.
The COC has been in negotiations for decades, and hammering out the agreement during this week’s meeting was a priority for the bloc’s current chair, the Philippines, a country with an exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, that significantly overlaps the territory claimed by China within its nine-dash line. Philippines foreign minister Ma. Theresa Lazaro on Nov. 15 told reporters that about 80% of a draft of the code had been completed.
But the agreement will have to wait until at least next year, when the next ASEAN meeting will be held in Singapore.
The overlapping claims of China and the Philippines in the South China Sea.
(AFP) Laos as an ASEAN member state wields significant influence despite not having any claims in the South China Sea, as the bloc operates on a consensus system. Vientiane’s deepening economic and military ties with China could make it sympathetic to Beijing’s foreign policy goals, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“For China, having a sympathetic voice within ASEAN could therefore be useful, particularly in shaping the language and provisions of the eventual agreement, rather than necessarily obstructing the negotiations outright,” he said.
Influence does not mean control
Kristanto said Laos could influence ASEAN’s collective position by objecting to clauses supported by claimant countries, but he cautioned against treating that capacity, or its growing relationship with China, as proof that it was exercising influence at Beijing’s direction.
“While its growing economic and military ties with China could give Beijing considerable influence, I’d say that currently there is insufficient evidence to conclude that Vientiane is deliberately obstructing the COC negotiations on Beijing’s behalf,” he said.
Laos also has interests that could limit its alignment with China, particularly its longstanding political and security relationship with Vietnam and its standing within ASEAN, Kristanto added.
Although the bloc’s charter establishes consultation and consensus as its basic decision-making principle, it also allows the ASEAN summit to decide how a specific decision can be made when consensus fails. Additionally, disagreements over sensitive issues can complicate a common position.
An Oct. 12, 2025, photo distributed by the Philippine Coast Guard shows a China coast guard ship, right, deploying a water cannon at a Philippine Bureau of Fisheries vessel near Thitu Island in disputed waters of the South China Sea.
(Philippine Coast Guard via AFP) Still, if in future negotiations China were to push for a less binding code and faced resistance, Laos could oppose ASEAN decisions or joint statements to help reshape the agreement, Enrico Cau, a Taipei-based independent security researcher, told RFA.
“Much like Cambodia, Laos seems to be closely aligned to China,” said Cau.
He explained that Chinese investment and expanding security ties support a relationship that also serves the interests of Lao and Cambodian leaders: alignment with Beijing could help sustain their governments and support development without requiring democratic reforms.
Cau therefore saw little reason to expect either country to make a fundamental shift away from supporting China within ASEAN. His assessment pointed to potential influence over future decisions, rather than identifying a specific Lao intervention in the current negotiations.
A different regional climate
Comparisons with Cambodia draw on the breakdown of an ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting in Phnom Penh in 2012. The meeting ended without a joint communiqué for the first time in the bloc’s history after disagreements over South China Sea language. Manila accused Cambodia, then the chair, of opposing references to Beijing taking control of Scarborough Shoal, a maritime feature within the Philippines’ EEZ.
Cambodia at that time described it as a “bilateral dispute” rather than a multilateral issue involving the whole of ASEAN.
Phnom Penh continued to veto drafts of the communiqué that included mentions of the shoal, Manila refused to sign off on versions that excluded it, and the meeting concluded in disagreement.
The following year, the Philippines took the issue to an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague, which issued a ruling in 2016 that invalidated Beijing’s claims based on the nine-dash line. China has rejected the ruling and continues to control the shoal.
Although Cambodia blocked an ASEAN communiqué that would have criticized China in 2012, the bloc is less likely to criticize China these days, Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore and non-resident scholar at Carnegie China, told RFA.
“Laos could take a blocking role but the context is somewhat different,” he said. “There is less appetite across ASEAN for criticizing Beijing today.”
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., center, and first lady Louise Araneta-Marcos, right, greet Laos Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith and his wife Alouny Kommasith upon arriving for the 49th ASEAN Summit, in Manila, Philippines, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026
(Ezra Acayan/Getty Images via AP) Unpredictability in the U.S. alongside China’s ability and willingness to exert pressure on ASEAN has made the bloc’s governments less willing to openly differ with Beijing, with the Philippines a notable exception, Chong said.
While most of the ASEAN member states have publicly stated their commitments to a substantive code of conduct, Chong questioned whether this was in fact the case. Some might wish to appear cooperative while remaining lukewarm about an agreement whose obligations and enforcement were unclear, he said.
That uncertainty could complicate efforts to distinguish Chinese influence through Laos from wider disagreements within ASEAN itself, according to Chong.
Both Washington and Beijing have in the past made efforts to secure Lao support for their respective Southeast Asia policy goals. During Laos’s ASEAN chairmanship in 2016, then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited Vientiane and emphasized ASEAN unity and maritime rights. Months later, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi publicly claimed support from Laos, Cambodia and Brunei for resolving maritime disputes through talks among directly concerned countries.
ASEAN Philippines: key takeaways
For future South China Sea negotiations, the analysts said that Laos’s role must also be judged against what an eventual code would achieve.
Chong said a largely declaratory agreement would likely have limited effects on China’s behavior at sea, meaning Laos’s actions might make less difference than the underlying weaknesses of the document. Cau argued that an initial agreement could still provide a foundation for improvements over time.
Kristanto said the central question was whether Laos could influence the substance of the eventual agreement, rather than simply delay its completion.
“After all, concluding a COC and concluding an effective COC are two different things, particularly when contentious issues such as its legal status, geographical scope, and implementation remain unresolved.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Declines in Asia as Nvidia results fail to reassure
articles.excerpt: Local and mainland shares were mixed at the start of trade on Wednesday as equities failed to capitalise on blockbuster…
articles.fullText:
Local and mainland shares were mixed at the start of trade on Wednesday as equities failed to capitalise on blockbuster earnings from Nvidia that soothed concerns about the AI boom, but have been overshadowed by the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang who admitted to a bunch of extra-marital affairs.

In Hong Kong, Hang Seng Index lost 79 points, or 0.34 percent, to open at 23,428.

Up north, shares began the day higher with the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index up 0.33 percent while the Shenzhen Component Index opened 0.37 percent higher.

In a highly anticipated earnings release on Tuesday, US tech giant Nvidia said third-quarter revenue topped expectations and doubled to more than US$115 billion while net profit hit US$65.3 billion.

The firm also increased its forecast for next year's revenue, predicting 75 percent growth, compared with a previous forecast of 70 percent.

Still, despite the positive results, Japan's Nikkei average reversed early gains to trade lower, as concerns about the outlook for AI development in the US and Nvidia's leadership outweighed the chip maker's robust outlook.

The Nikkei was down 0.72 percent, after earlier rising as much as 1.3 percent.

The broader Topix also turned lower, down 1.02 percent.

Nvidia shares rose nearly five percent in after-hours trading after the chipmaker, seen as a bellwether for the AI sector, reported quarterly revenue above forecasts in its first earnings report since Huang's abrupt departure as CEO this month.

Also, Nvidia's leadership signalled they would brook no dissent in their plan to find a new CEO, rejecting a "Stand With Jensen" campaign from allies of Huang, even as the Wall Street Journal reported a regulator was probing Nvidia.

"The momentum in Japan that was lifted by a strong outlook for Nvidia did not last long. The market was concerned about the fate of Jensen Huang," said Kazuaki Shimada, chief strategist at IwaiCosmo Securities.

"And a possible slowdown of US data centre construction weighed on investor sentiment, while the market also wanted to wait to see how Anthropic's IPO would proceed," he said. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Xi urges efforts to build a prosperous Asia-Pacific
articles.excerpt: President Xi Jinping on Wednesday said China is willing to work with all parties to forge ahead with greater confidence…
articles.fullText:
President Xi Jinping on Wednesday said China is willing to work with all parties to forge ahead with greater confidence and resolve to jointly build an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together.

Xi made the remarks in a keynote speech at the Apec CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen.

The president called for maintaining peace and stability – and building a bridge of openness and cooperation – for the Asia-Pacific to prosper together.

"Stability brings security; security brings prosperity," Xi said.

"The Asia-Pacific economy has maintained a stable and positive trajectory, becoming a key engine of global economic growth thanks to a long-term stable regional environment. The more complex the external situation becomes, the more resolutely we must uphold the post-war international order."

He said the region should support free and open trade and investment, adding that efforts should be made to eliminate trade and investment barriers to foster an open Asia-Pacific economy.

"History shows that openness brings progress, while isolation inevitably leads to backwardness. We must resolutely uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organisation at its core, support free and open trade and investment, and safeguard the stability and smooth functioning of global industrial and supply chains."

Xi called for efforts to steadily advance the process of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific.

Xi stressed the need to inject momentum into innovation-driven growth, and that efforts should be made to develop sci-tech innovation partnerships, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence, and promote green and low-carbon transition.

He called on the region to expand pathways to mutual benefits and win-win outcomes to prosper together.

Xi said China supports the establishment of a world association for bay areas economic cooperation, so as to deepen exchanges and interactions among various bay areas and explore new paths of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation.

"The Asia-Pacific region is home to the world's most important bay areas notable for their open and interconnected economies with positive spillover effects."

He also urged resolving differences through dialogue and consultation, and addressing challenges through solidarity and coordination.

The president added that China's 15th Five-Year Plan presents a list of opportunities for economic growth of the Asia-Pacific and beyond, describing the development blueprint as an invitation for cooperation extended to the global business community.

China will provide the global business community with its super-sized, open market, broad development prospects, as well as a cooperative environment that promotes mutual progress, he said.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Pochettino ends USA tenure, heads to Manchester
articles.excerpt: Mauricio Pochettino's reign as United States coach ended with a simple 2-0 win over Haiti on Tuesday, sent off in…
articles.fullText:
Mauricio Pochettino's reign as United States coach ended with a simple 2-0 win over Haiti on Tuesday, sent off in style by a Christian Pulisic bicycle kick as he heads to his new role at Manchester United.

Teenager Julian Hall also added his fifth goal from six games to secure an 8-0 aggregate victory in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final second leg in Cincinnati, with Pochettino set to fly to England just hours after the final whistle.

Pochettino, who steered the US to the last-16 of a home World Cup this summer, picked a strong lineup for his swansong and his favoured stars appeared determined to wave their coach off with a win, beginning with high intensity.

A bright Weston McKennie missed two good early chances, before turning creator in the 25th minute for Pulisic's opener.

Pulisic stole possession on the halfway line and surged up the left flank before feeding the ball inside.

McKennie crossed back into the box from the right and Pulisic, running away from goal, improvised a bicycle kick over his left shoulder that bounced in off the far post.

Striker Hall doubled the lead in the 43rd minute. McKennie again provided the assist, chipping the ball over the Haitian backline.

Hall did well to trap the ball, chest it down and then lift it over the goalkeeper. The 18-year-old has scored on all four US starts.

After the break Auston Trusty had a header acrobatically cleared off the line by Martin Experience. Video replays seemed to show it crossing over, but no goal was awarded.

Defensive midfielder Sebastian Berhalter picked up a yellow for a sliding challenge that rules him out of the semi-final in March.

Alex Freeman, the 22-year-old defender given his debut by Pochettino who has become a stalwart at right-back, did superbly to intercept a clear-cut chance for Josue Casimir.

Hall's header in the final few minutes bounced off the crossbar.

The often emotional Pochettino, who had issued a message before the game thanking US fans "from the bottom of my heart", calmly applauded Pulisic's spectacular strike, before exchanging warm hugs and smiles with his staff at the final whistle.

More testing challenges lie ahead, with United languishing in 18th place in the Premier League and due to face bitter rivals Liverpool on Sunday.

Pochettino is expected to head directly to United's Carrington training facility on arrival. (AFP)

Edited by Nazvi Careem

articles.title: Island Line gradually resumes after disruption
articles.excerpt: The MTR said on Wednesday morning that services on the Island Line were disrupted because of a signal equipment fault…
articles.fullText:
The MTR said on Wednesday morning that services on the Island Line were disrupted because of a signal equipment fault near the HKU station.

The railway operator said trains passing through the section must slow down, and overall journey times are expected to take an extra five to eight minutes.

It urged passengers to allow ample time for their journeys.

The MTR said services gradually resumed to normal at around 10.30am, about two hours after the incident was reported.
